query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor tin (Sn) addition (about 1–5 at.%) into cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance by enabling the formation of a continuous, adherent, Sn‐enriched oxide scale that suppresses pest oxidation without degrading its intrinsic room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room‐temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength in the range of 163–530 MPa at high temperatures.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a minor alloying addition of tin (Sn) (approximately 1–5 atomic percent) during melting and casting.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at approximately 800 °C for about 5 hours under load conditions that do not introduce significant creep or additional degradation.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, continuous, and adherent Sn‐rich oxide layer at the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, the added tin preferentially segregates to the surface where it oxidizes to form a Sn‐enriched oxide. This protective scale acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress, reducing the rate of pest oxidation while maintaining the underlying BCC microstructure and mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the Sn-modified HfNbTaTiZr is expected to show a marked reduction in oxidation (with fewer signs of pesting) after a 5-hour air exposure at around 800 °C while preserving similar levels of room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance (pest oxidation) under similar high-temperature air exposure despite its acceptable mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: This protective effect is anticipated for as-cast alloys exposed in air at around 800 °C for durations on the order of 5 hours. The behavior under significantly different temperatures, atmospheres, or after additional thermomechanical processing remains unverified.
generation.uncertainty: Although preliminary evidence supports the role of tin in enhancing oxidation resistance, the optimal tin concentration and long-term stability of the Sn-enriched oxide scale require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set with a 1–5 at.% tin addition and a control set without tin. Expose both sets to air at approximately 800 °C for 5 hours under identical loading conditions. After exposure, use scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to examine the oxide scales. Additionally, measure weight gains to quantify oxidation and perform room-temperature tensile and high-temperature yield strength tests.
measurements: Morphology, continuity, and chemical composition of the oxide layer (via SEM, EDS, XRD)
Weight gain associated with oxidation
Room-temperature tensile ductility
High-temperature yield strength (around 1000 °C)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-modified alloy does not form a more continuous and adherent Sn-enriched oxide scale (or shows similar pest oxidation levels as the control) or if its room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength are significantly reduced compared to the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. The oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys was improved dramatically when the key alloying elements Al, Cr, Si, and Ti were in synergy with other transition and refractory metals, for example Hf, Mo, and simple metal and metalloid elements, e.g., Sn [,,,,]. In the case of Sn, the early research [,] concentrated on alloys where its concentration was low to avoid the formation of the A15-Nb3Sn compound. In 2007, Geng et al [] reported that the addition

The research on the oxidation of Nb-silicide-based alloys would suggest (a) that Ge and/or Sn are needed to suppress pest oxidation, and (b) that, when these alloying additions were present individually or simultaneously in the alloys, the spallation of their scales at high temperatures was not suppressed. It is now well established that Ge or Sn has an effect on macrosegregation and can also reduce the liquidus temperature of the alloy. Alloying with Sn can affect the stability of the Nbss but not the alloying with Ge, which can, however, significantly reduce the cracking of the substrate below the scale/substrate interface []. Unfortunately, from the oxidation research on multicomponent Nb-silicide-based alloys, it is not clear whether it was the synergy of Sn or Ge individually or simultaneously with Al, Cr, Si, and Ti that improved oxidation resistance, or whether the presence of oxygen scavenging Hf with/without transition and refractory metals and with some or all of the aforementioned elements was essential for increasing the oxidation resistance.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a small, controlled amount of aluminum to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr (either through alloying or via a surface pack aluminization process) will promote the in situ formation of a thin, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale during high-temperature exposure, thereby markedly improving the alloy’s oxygen resistance without compromising its room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy displaying 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C with known oxidation issues (pesting) in air.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a minor addition of aluminum into the HfNbTaTiZr system (either through direct alloying or by applying a surface aluminization treatment).
drafts.conditions: Exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 hours under moderate loading conditions that do not induce significant creep, preserving essential mechanical properties.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent, and slow-growing alumina (Al2O3) scale on the alloy’s surface.
drafts.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, the added aluminum diffuses to the surface and oxidizes preferentially to form a protective alumina layer. This layer acts as a diffusion barrier, dramatically reducing further oxygen ingress and preventing the rapid oxidation (pesting) observed in the untreated alloy.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The Al-treated alloy will exhibit enhanced oxygen resistance (minimal pesting and reduced oxidation rate) under the test conditions compared to the untreated alloy, with retention of its mechanical properties (tensile ductility and yield strength).
drafts.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which undergoes pesting and surface degradation upon prolonged exposure to air at elevated temperatures.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under conditions of air exposure at around 800 °C for durations up to 5 hours and under stress conditions that do not markedly alter the alloy’s intrinsic mechanical behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy with a minor aluminum addition (via either bulk alloying or a surface aluminization treatment) and a control set without aluminum modification. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours while applying moderate load conditions. Following exposure, characterize the oxidation scale formation, measure the degree of oxidation (e.g., weight gain), and perform mechanical tests (tensile and yield measurements) on both sets.
measurements: Surface analysis (SEM/EDS, XRD) to determine the presence, continuity, and composition of the protective alumina scale
Weight-gain measurements to quantify oxidation rate
Mechanical testing for room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength before and after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-treated samples do not form a coherent alumina scale, if the oxidation rate and pesting behavior are not significantly reduced compared to the untreated samples, or if the mechanical properties degrade beyond acceptable limits, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of aluminum (e.g., ~1 at.%) to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will result in the formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale during high-temperature oxidation that improves oxygen resistance without significantly degrading the alloy’s room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with poor oxygen resistance.
drafts.intervention: Minor alloying addition of aluminum (approximately 1 at.%) to the base composition.
drafts.conditions: Exposure to air at 800 °C for 5 hours.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous and adherent Al2O3 (alumina) scale on the alloy surface.
drafts.mechanism: Aluminum has a strong affinity for oxygen and forms a stable alumina layer. This protective scale acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen, significantly slowing down further oxidation without substantially altering the overall phase composition or mechanical properties of the alloy.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The aluminized alloy will exhibit significantly improved oxidation resistance (thinner, more coherent oxide scale and reduced bulk oxidation) during a 5-hour exposure to air at 800 °C while maintaining comparable room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (within the 163–530 MPa range).
drafts.baseline: Untreated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr oxidizes rapidly in air at 800 °C, leading to substantial oxygen ingress and degradation of mechanical properties over similar timescales.
drafts.boundary: Applicable primarily for oxidation conditions at 800 °C in air with a 5-hour exposure; mechanical and oxidation performance is considered for conditions where the original alloy properties (room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength) are observed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr as the control, and one set modified with approximately 1 at.% Al. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours under identical conditions. Post-exposure, assess the surface oxide scale morphology (via SEM/EDS and XRD) as well as room temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity
Chemical composition and phase identification of the oxide layer
Room-temperature tensile ductility
High-temperature yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminized alloy does not exhibit a significantly reduced oxide scale thickness (e.g., less than an 8–16% relative improvement) or if its mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) are degraded by more than approximately 10% compared to the untreated alloy after exposure, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of tin (Sn) as an alloying addition (e.g. on the order of 1–5 at.%) to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a Sn-enriched, adherent, and slow-growing oxide layer that retards pest oxidation without degrading its room‐temperature ductility or high‐temperature strength.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy with its native single-phase BCC structure and mechanical properties as reported (8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility; yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
drafts.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding a trace level of tin (Sn), e.g. 1–5 at.%, during melting/casting.
drafts.conditions: Exposure in air at elevated temperatures around 800 °C for durations on the order of 5 hours, with the requirement that the mechanical performance (room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength) is preserved.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense, adherent Sn-enriched oxide scale at the surface of the alloy.
drafts.mechanism: Tin acts as a reactive element that segregates to the oxide–metal interface and enriches the scale with Sn; this modifies the oxide growth kinetics (by reducing oxygen diffusion rates through the scale) and increases scale adhesion, thereby suppressing pest oxidation without significantly altering the underlying BCC matrix and its mechanical performance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the Sn-modified alloy will exhibit a significantly reduced rate of oxygen uptake, delayed or suppressed onset of pest oxidation during 5-hour air exposure at 800 °C, and maintain similarly high room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
drafts.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy shows inadequate oxygen resistance (prone to pest oxidation) under the same conditions.
drafts.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected in the temperature range around 800 °C for exposures up to about 5 hours; significant deviations in temperature, longer exposure times, or excessive Sn addition might alter phase stability or mechanical properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloys: one set with the addition of a low level of Sn (1–5 at.%) and a control set without Sn. Subject both sets to air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours. Characterize the surface oxide scale (via SEM/EDS and XRD) and measure weight gain. Perform tensile tests at room temperature and high-temperature (around 1000 °C) on both sets to compare ductility and yield strength.
measurements: Weight gain due to oxidation
Oxide scale thickness and composition (Sn content presence in oxide)
Surface morphology (presence or absence of pest oxidation features)
Room-temperature tensile elongation
High-temperature yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation rate (e.g., similar weight gain and pest oxidation features) or if its mechanical properties (ductility and high-temperature yield strength) deteriorate compared to the control alloy under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of tin (Sn) – on the order of 5 atomic percent – to the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy will improve its oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a protective, adherent Sn-rich oxide scale during high‐temperature exposure without significantly degrading its room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical properties.
drafts.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with 8–16% room‐temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
drafts.intervention: Introduce ~5 at.% Sn into the alloy composition during melting and casting.
drafts.conditions: Exposure in air at approximately 800 °C for 5 hours, while requiring that both the room‐temperature tensile ductility and the high-temperature yield strength remain within the useful performance range.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous and adherent Sn-rich oxide layer at the alloy surface that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
drafts.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, the added Sn segregates to the surface and participates in oxide-scale formation. This Sn-rich oxide improves scale adhesion and reduces oxygen ingress, thereby suppressing the rapid oxidation or pesting observed in the unmodified alloy, while the bulk BCC structure is maintained to preserve mechanical performance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated equiatomic alloy, the Sn-modified alloy will exhibit significantly improved oxygen resistance (e.g., reduced pest oxidation) under an 800 °C, 5-hour air exposure while retaining a similar level of room-temperature ductility and high-temperature strength.
drafts.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr shows inadequate oxygen resistance during a 5-hour air exposure at 800 °C despite having useful mechanical properties.
drafts.boundary: This improvement is expected to hold for the cast state in air at around 800 °C over exposure durations on the order of 5 hours; the effects at significantly different temperatures, atmospheres, or after extensive thermomechanical processing remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: (1) the baseline equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and (2) a modified alloy with ~5 at.% Sn addition produced under identical casting conditions. Expose samples from both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, characterize the oxide layer using SEM, EDS, and XRD, and measure the onset of pest oxidation. Additionally, perform room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., yield strength at 1000 °C) to compare mechanical properties.
measurements: Morphology and continuity of the oxide scales (via SEM)
Chemical composition of the oxide layers (via EDS)
Phase composition of oxide scales (via XRD)
Extent of pest oxidation (e.g., weight gain, scale spallation)
Room-temperature tensile ductility

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-added alloy does not form a more continuous, adherent, and protective Sn-enriched oxide scale—as evidenced by similar or worse pest oxidation indicators—and if its room-temperature or high-temperature mechanical properties are significantly degraded compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.
